fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. The Rabshakeh says Hezekiah tells them, "The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria." That's the Rabshakeh's report of Hezekiah's words. Right after it he says, "Do not listen to Hezekiah…"

Yes, baker. The text says, "…the people remained silent and did not answer a word…" After all that shouting, nobody says anything back. The reason comes in the same verse: Hezekiah had commanded, "Do not answer him."
That's right, baker. The people stayed silent because Hezekiah had commanded, "Do not answer him." The people followed the king's order.
Ahaz isn't the king in this scene, friend. The people were silent because Hezekiah had commanded, "Do not answer him." Hezekiah is the king giving the order here.
Uzziah isn't named in this passage, baker. The one who gave the order is the king in this story. Hezekiah had commanded, "Do not answer him." It's Hezekiah's word the people are keeping.

Right on target, baker. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian royal officer, is sent "…to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem." Hezekiah is king of Judah, and Jerusalem is where he is. On the way, the Rabshakeh stops by the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the Launderer's Field.

Hebron isn't in this passage at all, baker. The text names the destination plainly: the Rabshakeh is sent to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. Hebron is a fair guess, and I've mixed up oven temperatures plenty of times myself.

Brave is a kind word, friend, and I don't think the Rabshakeh is in a kind-word mood. He says, "You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words." Empty is the word he picks. I don't think he's handing out compliments.
Wise isn't the word he uses, baker. In his words, "…these are empty words." That's what he calls Hezekiah's strategy and strength for war.
Moab isn't mentioned in his speech, baker. The nation he names is Egypt: "Look now, you are trusting in Egypt…" He even mentions Pharaoh king of Egypt.

A wall is a good guess with the story set in a city, friend, but he reaches for something else. He says Egypt is "…that splintered reed of a staff…" It's something you lean on, and it pierces the hand of anyone who does.

A dry well makes a solid picture, baker, but it isn't his. The Rabshakeh calls Egypt "…that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it." His picture is a staff, not a well, and it pierces the hand that leans on it.
True, baker, that's what he claims. He says, "The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’…" Notice that it's the Rabshakeh saying this about himself.

Yes, baker. They say, "Do not speak to us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall." They ask him to speak Aramaic instead, since they understand it. The Rabshakeh later mentions the men sitting on the wall too.
No hill in this scene, baker. The request is, "Do not speak to us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall." I think it's the people on the wall they have in mind.
The text says the opposite, friend. The Rabshakeh "…stood and called out loudly in Hebrew…" That means Hebrew, and loud.
Opening the gates isn't in this scene, baker. The text says, "…the people remained silent and did not answer a word…" Silence is what the people give him.
You got it, baker. The text says they "…relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh." They came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn when they did it.
Egypt is the Rabshakeh's topic, baker, not theirs. The text says the three men "…relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh." They pass along his message, and Egypt isn't mentioned in that verse.
